purpose: Add reusable teaching, proclamation and eschatological scenes that recur across high-value comparator relations.

scenes.title: The narrow gate inside the Sermon on the Mount's closing choices
scenes.summary: Near the end of the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus contrasts a narrow gate and difficult way leading to life with a broad way leading to destruction, then continues with warnings about false prophets, false profession and the need to do what he has taught.
scenes.setting: Galilean teaching setting within the Sermon on the Mount
scenes.lead_in: Matthew 5-7 presents a sustained body of Jesus' teaching on kingdom character, prayer, judgment, trust and practice.
scenes.outcome: The gate image is embedded in an ethical and practical call to follow a demanding way, not merely in a spatial map of heaven.
scenes.what_follows: Matthew moves from the sermon into narratives of healing, discipleship and authority.
scenes.historical_context: The scene belongs to Matthew's presentation of Jesus as authoritative teacher within first-century Jewish moral and scriptural discourse.
scenes.literary_context: Matthew 7 closes the Sermon on the Mount with paired alternatives that force a response to the preceding teaching.
scenes.textual_or_translation_caveats: The image is metaphorical teaching language; later traditions often expand it into detailed eschatological geography not stated in the verses themselves.
counterreadings_or_limits: The text does not describe two human guardians flanking the gate.
The narrow gate does not by itself identify a modern person, place or structure.

scenes.title: Bread of Life discourse after the feeding of the crowd
scenes.summary: After the feeding of the five thousand, the crowd seeks Jesus. He redirects attention from perishable bread to enduring life, identifies himself as the Bread of Life and develops increasingly difficult language about eating his flesh and drinking his blood, after which many followers withdraw.
scenes.setting: Capernaum area after the feeding sign
scenes.lead_in: John 6 begins with a large crowd being fed from a small amount of bread and fish, followed by Jesus crossing the sea.
sequence: Jesus identifies as Bread of Life
scenes.outcome: Bread moves from physical provision to a demanding claim about Jesus' life-giving identity and participation in him.
scenes.what_follows: John 7 moves into festival conflict and further disputes about Jesus' identity and origin.
scenes.historical_context: The discourse draws on Jewish scriptural manna traditions and is narrated within John's distinctive sign-and-discourse theology.
scenes.literary_context: John interprets a feeding sign through a long identity discourse in which material bread becomes a vehicle for claims about life, belief and participation.
scenes.textual_or_translation_caveats: Christian traditions differ sharply over sacramental readings of the flesh-and-blood language; the comparator should not collapse those debates.
counterreadings_or_limits: Calling an object 'bread' in a modern symbolic system does not make it equivalent to Jesus in John 6.

scenes.title: The grain of wheat must die to bear much fruit
scenes.summary: When Greeks seek Jesus, he announces that the hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified and uses a grain of wheat that falls into the earth and dies as an image for fruitfulness. The saying is embedded in teaching about losing life, service, judgment and being lifted up.
scenes.lead_in: Jesus has entered Jerusalem; public attention and conflict are intensifying as Passover approaches.
scenes.outcome: The seed image interprets impending death as a transition toward multiplied life and is inseparable from the Passion trajectory.
scenes.what_follows: John turns toward unbelief, Isaiah citations and the final pre-Passion teaching sequence.
scenes.historical_context: The saying is preserved in John's Passion-oriented theology rather than as a general botanical teaching.
scenes.literary_context: John 12 functions as a hinge between Jesus' public ministry and the Farewell/Passion material; death and glorification are tightly coupled.
scenes.textual_or_translation_caveats: The text says a grain dies and bears fruit; later symbolic applications to specific crops or persons are interpretive extensions.
counterreadings_or_limits: A modern experience of loss or transformation is not established as salvific merely by resemblance to the grain metaphor.

scenes.title: Paul's received proclamation: death for sins, burial, resurrection and witnesses
scenes.summary: Paul reminds the Corinthian community of the gospel he says he received and delivered: Christ died for sins, was buried, was raised on the third day and appeared to Cephas, the Twelve, a large group, James, the apostles and finally Paul.
scenes.setting: Pauline argument to the Corinthian church
scenes.lead_in: Earlier chapters address community disputes, worship and spiritual gifts; chapter 15 turns to resurrection because some deny resurrection of the dead.
scenes.outcome: Resurrection is presented as a witnessed proclamation foundational to Paul's larger argument that resurrection of the dead matters for Christian faith.
scenes.what_follows: Paul argues at length about resurrection, transformed bodies, Adam/Christ and final victory over death.
scenes.historical_context: 1 Corinthians is a first-century Pauline letter; 15:3-7 is widely studied as an early received formula or tradition, though scholars debate details of its pre-Pauline form.
scenes.literary_context: The witness list is the opening evidence frame for Paul's much larger resurrection argument in 1 Corinthians 15.
scenes.textual_or_translation_caveats: The passage reports appearances as part of proclamation; it does not provide modern forensic standards for evaluating unrelated resurrection claims.
counterreadings_or_limits: Using resurrection vocabulary about a modern event does not make that event the resurrection proclaimed by Paul.
A claim of witnesses still requires independent evaluation of who witnessed what.

scenes.title: Ascension in a cloud and the promise of Jesus' return
scenes.summary: After appearing to the apostles, Jesus speaks about the kingdom and the coming Spirit, is lifted up and taken from their sight by a cloud. Two figures tell the disciples that Jesus will come in the same way they saw him go, after which the group returns to Jerusalem to wait and pray.
scenes.setting: near Jerusalem, followed by an upper room gathering
scenes.lead_in: Luke's Gospel has ended with resurrection appearances and blessing; Acts reopens the transition from Jesus' ministry to the apostolic mission.
sequence: two men announce return in same manner
scenes.outcome: Departure and promised return are coupled to a mission of witness empowered by the Spirit.
scenes.what_follows: The disciples replace Judas and then receive the Spirit at Pentecost in Acts 2.
scenes.historical_context: Acts is the second volume of Luke-Acts and narrates the transition from Jesus to the early church's Spirit-empowered mission.
scenes.literary_context: The ascension functions as both closure and launch: Jesus departs while the narrative focus shifts to witnesses carrying the message outward.
scenes.textual_or_translation_caveats: The text links cloud, ascent and return but does not specify a modern calendar or geographic return point.
counterreadings_or_limits: Cloud imagery alone does not identify a particular modern person or weather event with the promised return.

scenes.title: Psalm 110: enthronement at the right hand and priestly kingship
scenes.summary: A royal figure is invited to sit at YHWH's right hand while enemies become a footstool; rule extends from Zion, and the figure is also declared a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.
scenes.setting: poetic royal and cultic imagery centered on Zion
scenes.lead_in: Psalm 110 stands within the Psalter as a compact royal oracle later quoted extensively in the New Testament.
scenes.outcome: Kingship, right-hand enthronement, enemy-subordination and priesthood are compressed into one influential psalm.
scenes.what_follows: Later Jewish and Christian interpretation repeatedly reuses the psalm, especially its opening right-hand saying and Melchizedek priesthood.
scenes.historical_context: The psalm likely arose from royal/temple traditions; the identity and original setting of 'my lord' are debated in scholarship.
scenes.literary_context: Its terse oracle structure made it unusually reusable in later messianic and Christological argument.
scenes.textual_or_translation_caveats: The Hebrew phrase translated 'my lord' and the psalm's original royal setting should be distinguished from later Christian application to Jesus.
counterreadings_or_limits: Footstool imagery is royal-poetic subordination language; it does not authorize dehumanizing modern opponents.

scenes.title: Revelation's opening cloud-coming announcement
scenes.summary: Revelation opens as a disclosure communicated through John, blesses readers and hearers, names Jesus as faithful witness and ruler, announces that he comes with clouds and every eye will see him, then moves into John's vision of the glorified Son-of-Man-like figure among lampstands.
scenes.setting: epistolary-apocalyptic opening from Patmos to seven churches
scenes.lead_in: The work identifies itself as revelation and prophecy intended for concrete communities in Roman Asia.
scenes.outcome: Cloud-coming, universal seeing, witness, kingship and visionary Son-of-Man imagery establish the book's opening theological frame.
scenes.what_follows: Messages are addressed to the seven churches before the vision shifts to the heavenly throne room.
scenes.historical_context: Revelation addresses first-century churches under Roman imperial conditions while using Jewish apocalyptic symbolism and scriptural allusion.
scenes.literary_context: The cloud-coming line is not isolated: it belongs to a prologue that immediately joins Jesus' witness, death, kingship and Daniel-like visionary imagery.
scenes.textual_or_translation_caveats: Apocalyptic imagery is symbolically dense; interpreters disagree over chronology and referents, so the line should not be treated as a simple weather prediction.
counterreadings_or_limits: A modern cloud metaphor or mashed-food joke can echo the wording playfully but does not establish fulfillment of Revelation 1:7.

scenes.title: The shoot from Jesse, Spirit-endowed ruler and peaceable kingdom
scenes.summary: Isaiah imagines a shoot from Jesse's stump upon whom YHWH's Spirit rests. This ruler judges with righteousness, a transformed peaceable order follows, and the Root of Jesse becomes a signal for peoples amid a wider restoration and gathering.
scenes.setting: prophetic vision of judgment, ideal rule and restoration
scenes.lead_in: Isaiah 10 has used tree-felling imagery for proud imperial power; chapter 11 answers the cut-down landscape with new growth from Jesse.
sequence: violent predation transformed in peace imagery
earth filled with knowledge of YHWH
scenes.outcome: Root, Spirit, righteous rule, nations and restoration become one prophetic complex later reused in messianic interpretation.
scenes.what_follows: Isaiah 12 offers a hymn of thanksgiving before the book moves into oracles concerning nations.
scenes.historical_context: The oracle emerges from Isaiah's monarchic and imperial-crisis world and was later reread messianically in Jewish and Christian traditions.
scenes.literary_context: The chapter deliberately reverses felled-tree imagery with new growth and links royal justice to cosmic/social peace and restoration.
scenes.textual_or_translation_caveats: 'Root of Jesse' and 'shoot from the stump of Jesse' are related images in the chapter but not identical botanical roles.
counterreadings_or_limits: Root imagery does not by itself identify a modern root/tree symbol with the Davidic ruler.

scenes.title: John's first disciples name Jesus Lamb, Messiah, Son of God and Son of Man
scenes.summary: John the Baptist points to Jesus as Lamb of God; disciples begin following him, Andrew tells Simon that they have found the Messiah, Philip and Nathanael are called, and the sequence culminates in Son-of-God/King-of-Israel language and Jesus' promise of heaven opened with angels ascending and descending upon the Son of Man.
scenes.setting: Jordan-region witness scenes followed by early disciple calling
scenes.lead_in: John's prologue has introduced Word, light, witness and incarnation before John the Baptist denies being the Messiah and identifies himself as a witness.
sequence: Nathanael confesses Son of God/King of Israel
Jesus promises opened heaven and angelic movement on Son of Man
scenes.outcome: Multiple titles accumulate around Jesus before the Gospel's sign narrative begins, linking messianic recognition with Jacob-ladder imagery.
scenes.what_follows: John 2 begins the Cana sign and temple episode, developing sign, glory and identity themes.
scenes.historical_context: The scene reflects Johannine theological presentation of early disciples and messianic titles within a first-century Jewish scriptural world.
scenes.literary_context: John stacks identity titles rapidly so later signs and discourses develop claims already introduced in the opening chapter.
scenes.textual_or_translation_caveats: 'Messiah' is explicitly glossed as 'Christ' in the narrative; the later project term 'Moshiach' is linguistically related but not evidence of identity.
counterreadings_or_limits: Using Messiah/Moshiach vocabulary in a modern project does not establish that the speaker is the figure identified in John 1.
